CALL FOR INDUSTRY MEETING TO IMPROVE GRAIN MOVEMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, 1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Developments in several country elevator points reveal a complete breakdown in car allocation and co-ordination within the grain handling and transportation system. Last week in Alberta, the points of St. Paul, Fort Saskatchewan and Bonny-ville were allocated several cars for which there were no orders. These cars remained on sidings for a week and subsequently were returned empty, in spite of the fact that the elevators were full of grain. Today this has been repeated again at the delivery point of St. Paul that received more cars for which there are no orders. Whether these developments are occurring by design or through sheer incompetence is not known. What is known is that this disorder and chaos must be resolved without further delay. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton):
That the Minister of Transport act immediately to convene an "emergency grain summit" which would draw together representatives of all components of the grain handling, marketing and transportation system to deal with this crisis and to arrive at solutions in the presence of all parties concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the announcement of the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) of a consultative committee on the implications of telecommunications for Canadian sovereignty, which is supposed to produce specific recommendations on the restructuring of the Canadian telecommunications system by the first week of February, 1979, and that this monumental task involving the public domain is to be performed behind closed doors without public participation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That the terms of reference of this committee be expanded to at least have representative public briefs from interested parties to give some validity to the exercise, otherwise the government acknowledge that this complex and fundamental issue should be the subject matter of a proper royal commission, so that the public will not have the impression that the just society of years ago has now become the closed society.

subsubtopic: FUNCTIONS OF NEW MINISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the new President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. I see he has just arrived. There is a good deal of public confusion about the role and the responsibilities of this new minister. The original press release indicated that he had responsibility for reviewing and approving-and, therefore, presumably, disapproving-policies and legislation emanating from the constituent ministries.
On the CTV program Question Period, the minister said he had a co-ordinating role, which is something quite different. Perhaps this confusion could be cleared up if the minister would indicate to the House just what functions he will be performing in his new ministry which heretofore have not been performed. After all, there is a cabinet committee; there are responsibilities in the Privy Council office and the Prime Minister's office for co-ordinating. subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who I am pleased to hear has at least been left with what the president of the new economic board calls global economic policy. My question happens to touch on global economic policy, namely, the state of our sagging dollar.
As another $600 million was lost in the month of November, causing the dollar to fall another half cent today, would the Minister of Finance, who presumably can still speak on this subject, tell us how he explains this sad phenomenon?

subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the month of November was an extraordinary month because of the move made by the American government in relation to their own dollar. In spite of that, we have maintained the Canadian dollar at a reasonable level. Of course, in the figure published this morning there was a large number inscribed. However, one has to deduct from that the fact that if the American dollar has improved substantially during the course of the month, what the Canadian government holds in reserves in the form of SDRs has been reduced by that much. In spite of the big movement in the money market last month, the change in the reserve of the Canadian government has been less than $500 million.

subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: The Minister of Finance, in simple terms, has said that the Americans are doing much better in defending their dollar than we in Canada in defending our dollar. Even if you allow for the figure the Minister of Finance has referred to, we have still lost half a billion dollars in that one month. Will the minister indicate if he continues to feel that the management of our dollar remains in capable hands?

subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the fact that the Canadian dollar is fluctuating on international markets at this time is the consequence of a long established government policy whereby the level of the Canadian dollar, like most currencies of the western hemisphere, is determined by the market. I want to tell the hon. member that the fact that the Canadian dollar is much more competitive at this time gave many sectors of our economy the necessary stimulus to become competitive and increase our trade balance. In fact, the Canadian trade balance for 1978 will reach a record level.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: My final question to the Minister of Finance touches on his last answer in which he tried to glorify the cheap dollar as something of great benefit to Canada. Will the minister confirm the report, released by him to the first ministers, from the Economic Council of Canada which indicated that the cheap, 85-cent dollar is having disastrous effects on inflation in Canada, with certain corporate profits, for example, being as high as 97 per cent up, compared to last year, largely due to the minister's new, cheap 85-cent dollar?

subsubtopic: FURTHER DECLINE IN VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION

However, I must tell the hon. member that most of the effect of this problem with a reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar was absorbed in the last year and a half in the market. We can now see some stabilization in the rate of inflation. In fact, for the last three-month period we have had the lowest rate of inflation in years.

However, I think this does point out the difficulties we get into in situations of this kind. speechtext:
1.	What are the regulations, duties and responsibilities of the cable television operators with respect to political programming on the community channel?
2.	Are these regulations, duties and responsibilities applied equally to all candidates, regardless of party or non-party affiliation?
3.	What measures are available to regulate the political programming? What means are available to apprehend offenders of these regulations?

speakeroldname: Mr. C. Douglas (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: CABLE TELEVISION-POLITICAL PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Communications is concerned, the answer to the above question is as follows:
1.	The CRTC Cable Television Regulations (1976) state:
13.	(1) Where a licensee provides time on its community channel for the distribution of programming of a partisan political character, it shall allocate such time on an equitable basis to all political parties and rival candidates.
(2) Where a licensee and the political parties and candidates are unable to reach agreement as to what, in any particular circumstances, constitutes an equitable allocation of time by the licensee, the licensee may refer the dispute to the commission and the commission shall allocate the time as it considers appropriate in the circumstances.
14.	Where a licensee provides opportunity on its community channel for the expression of views on matters of public concern, it shall provide reasonable, balanced opportunity for the expression of differing views on such matters.
2.	As regulation 13. (1) states, the licensee shall allocate time "on an equitable basis to all political parties and rival candidates".
3.	Under the same regulations (section 12) each licensee is required for a period of four weeks after distribution to keep a written program log and to maintain the audio reproduction of all programming distributed on its community channel. This permits the commission the means to apprehend offenders of these regulations. These regulations constitute the basic minimum standards to which cable television licensees must adhere. Every licensee who violates the provisions of any applicable regulation is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction of a fine not exceeding twenty-five thousand dollars for a first offence and not exceeding fifty thousand dollars for each subsequent offence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Broadview has raised an important issue regarding the child tax credit bill that is now before us, and clause 4 specifically. The point he is raising is that, under the proposed legislation, married couples with children may be penalized in comparison to common-law couples who are in otherwise identical circumstances. I might say that this general issue did receive a fair degree of discussion at the time we were considering clause 1 and clause 2, and I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has spoken to it specifically as well. Both spouses in a legal marriage would have to report their incomes to apply for a credit, but in a common-law union only the income of one spouse would have to be reported.
At the outset, let me say that I am sympathetic to the view that, in principle, the tax treatment of persons in a common-law marriage should be no different from that of legally married persons. While the Income Tax Act does not now recognize common-law spouses, this does not reflect any moral judgment on the part of the government. Rather, it is a consequence of the difficulties of identifying and verifying who is a common-law spouse, for the purposes of many provisions of the Income Tax Act for which this is relevant.
The issue of tax treatment of common-law spouses is not something new that has just been created by our proposed child tax credit program. The proposed legislation is only following existing provisions elsewhere in the Income Tax Act. These provisions do raise complex issues in the case of common-law spouses and there are issues with which we have been grappling for some time. For example, in several provinces significant reforms in family law have been adopted or are under study. These family law reforms clearly have implications for the income tax system, and are continuing to be discussed by federal and provincial officials. The main point here is that the issues surrounding the tax treatment of common-law spouses are much broader that those raised by the proposed child tax credit.
On grounds of equity and fairness, it seems clear that common-law spouses should not be allowed to derive any special advantage from the child tax credit. However, from the broader perspective of the entire income tax system, it is not possible to say whether or not in general common-law spouses are better or worse off than legally married couples. Any such calculation would depend on many specific details of the couple's circumstances. For example, common-law spouses can use the equivalent to married exemption. On the other hand, the marital exemption cannot be claimed in respect of a common-law spouse, nor can the unused portions of the age exemption or the interest and pension deductions be transferred between common-law spouses.
While some of the family law reform legislation provides for support payments on marriage breakdown for both legally married and common-law spouses, periodic support payments are only tax deductible in the case of legal marriages. The impact of these kinds of provisions is a very complex set of financial advantages and disadvantages to being common law. In any case, I am quite sure that the net financial effect of

December 4, 1978

these provisions does not have any significant impact on the institution of marriage in this country.
It is true that a number of federal statutes do make some provisions for common-law spouses, for example, the Canada Pension Plan and the War Veterans Allowance Act. But let me point out that these two statutes have different definitions of who it is that qualifies as a common-law spouse. Furthermore, in these other federal statutes it is typically in the couple's interest to establish that they are common-law spouses. As we are all aware, it is the opposite situation with the proposed child tax credit. Thus, common-law couples will not want to come forward to prove that they are in fact living as if they were legally married.
Let us suppose, however, that we did want to treat common-law and legally married taxpayers identically for purposes of the child tax credit. How could this be done? First, some definition of common law would have to be chosen. This definition could require one year of cohabitation, though it may be preferable to require three or seven years, particularly if the children are from a previous marriage. We would then have to determine the precise date when cohabitation began. In many situations some degree of ministerial discretion would be necessary. But then how are we to determine when couples are actually cohabiting, if they spend at least three nights a week together? Finally, since common-law couples will, in most cases, not want to come forward with the required information, we face the question of enforcement. While there are no firm data on the number of common-law couples in Canada today, there are about one-half million single mothers, most of whom would be eligible to claim the credit. The government would clearly be in a difficult position if it had to verify that none of these women were actually living common-law. Thus, any definition based on a period of cohabitation would involve certain difficult and unpopular administrative procedures.
These problems, I hope and expect, will not be insurmountable; but they are difficult. Work is already under way on the issues raised by common-law marriages, particularly in the context of provincial family law reform. Federal finance officials are meeting their provincial counterparts next week to discuss precisely this issue. I think we would be well advised to proceed in a reasoned and cautious manner to deal with these complex issues. The new child tax credit, which will be of immediate benefit to millions of families, should not have to await their resolution.

Mr. Chairman, would it be permissible for me to add information on other government programs which I think is relevant?
Under the Canada Pension Plan the survivor's benefit is awarded to the surviving common-law spouse and we use documentary evidence proving residence and public representation. As to the split of pension credits, we recognize legal marriages only because of the practical problems of defining the beginning and the end of the relationship, and numerous possible subsequent relationships.
Family Allowances
Under the Old Age Pension Act, more precisely under the Guaranteed Income Supplement, we do recognize common-law marriages on the simple basis of a statutory declaration of the relationship.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan other than under provincial welfare programs, common-law relationships are recognized.
Basically what I heard the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance say is that marriage brings a lot of fiscal privileges, and Canadians living in a common-law situation do not benefit from them. For the first time it is the reverse situation that confronts us whereby what the Department of Finance estimates to be an insignificant number of women living in a common-law situation would benefit from the child tax credit, while the "husband", in terms of a common-law relationship, would be making too large a salary for the program. The Department of Finance estimates this number of Canadian mothers to be insignificant.
I guess the ideal is to study the common-law situations which we can recognize in order to find an operational definition. I understand a study is taking place at the present with the Department of Finance.

I can assure the House, the parliamentary secretary and the minister, that it is not with the enforcing aspect I was primarily concerned. I appreciate this might cause some administrative difficulties, but on this side of the House we want to be sure the redistributive effect of the proposal takes cognizance of the reality of the child's circumstances rather than the fiction of the child's circumstances.
I appreciate there are Fiscal and physical advantages and disadvantages to common law and legal marriages. I would have thought it might have been possible for the government, rather than waiting for a wholesale reform of the Income Tax Act-which we are not prepared to do on this side of the House-to start with this particular measure. It affects so many families across Canada. There is now a growing recognition by provincial governments that common-law relationships do exist and do create certain rights and certain obligations on the part of parents in a common-law marriage. Taking into account these changes in family law reform which are taking place right across the country from Newfoundland to British Columbia, I would have thought that it might have been possible to incorporate this amendment, or if you like, to have a definition of a common-law marriage for the purposes of this clause only. I would think that cohabitation for one year is all that is required.
We are not interested in proving whether it is a relationship of one night, three nights or seven nights. That is not the concern. The concern is to see whether or not there is an economic unit which is not being recognized by this law. It is

not a question of sexual cohabitation; that is irrelevant. What is relevant is whether there is an economic unit. Any definition will be arbitrary, but perhaps if we said there was cohabitation for a year that would be sufficient to establish that there was an element of support.
Personally I do not see any problem. Perhaps I could be enlightened further. I do not see any problem in saying that "for the purposes of this section and this act, a common-law relationship is as follows." Frankly, I do not know whether the redistributive problem is a minuscule or a serious problem. On this side we want to make sure that the redistributive effects of the act are held as an integrity. Mliss Begin: Mr. Chairman, perhaps 1 could answer my colleague from Broadview so as to convince him to withdraw his amendment. I will explain why. Such an amendment has to be tied in with a reform of the complete income tax system, otherwise it will not work. The idea of the New Democratic Party, rightly so, it seems to me, is to ensure that redistribution ends up in the right place. They say a few cases of common-law situations will permit mothers, in good economic circumstances to receive moneys which do not belong to them, because they are not recognized by the income tax system, to the detriment of other Canadian mothers. We think there is a case in that regard, but for only a very few mothers.
If we were to correct this bill right away, and through this bill recognize common-law situations, but without a change in the general Income Tax Act, it will result in trying to implement something that will not work. How would common-law couples establish the two sources of income, or the husband's source of income, when it plays against their own interest? All people are greedy, and function around money and economic advantages. While the whole income tax system does not give the fiscal privileges to common-law couples that it does to legal marriages, suddenly we would be asking a few mothers, most likely single mothers, to be more catholic than the Pope! One would be asking them to declare either the husband's income, or the two sources of income, and yet they would not get the tax privileges of the income tax system that are applicable to a legal marriage. These people will not do that, and we have no policing mechanism. That is the reason why the amendment will not work.
I have never understood why the Income Tax Act does not recognize common-law situations, and while I was minister of national revenue I asked that particular question many times. I was always told that it was a question of potential abuse. When I became Minister of National Health and Welfare I discovered almost all social programs do recognize the common-law situations. I wondered why we did not have abuses in the case of older people. I wondered if that was the mentality of Canadians, that we trust older people not to cheat the system through the GIS, and yet we do not trust young couples, for example, those students who enter into a trial

marriage for whatever reasons. I do know that consistency should be introduced into all of our programs. It is probable that the amount of abuse would be a small percentage of the total government programs, but I am not sure of that. That is an assumption.
I firmly believe a correction to this bill, C-10, that we are studying right now, will never be enforceable because the rest of the income tax system does not give couples in common-law relationships the same privileges that married people get. If they received the privileges of the whole of the income tax system then they must be ready to acknowledge the common-law situations when it comes to the child tax credit. This is the reason why 1 think this amendment suggested by the hon. member for Broadview is unenforceable. Because of that I think we should wait for an amendment to the whole Income Tax Act. I do not mean wait to pass Bill C-10. It should be put on the record that this is a problem we want to see dealt with and looked into quite seriously. It should not be tied to this particular bill because it will not work.

Mr. Chairman, 1 listened with interest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and particularly to the last part of her remarks which I thought were the most worth-while, lucid comments that she has made in this whole matter, that is to say, that we should wait for some amendments to the whole of the Income Tax Act before we start tinkering with what is a very basic proposal.
I am quite fascinated by the twists and turns of the minister's response in this whole issue. She said at one point that almost ail programs of National Health and Welfare recognize the common-law situation. Then she backed off and said that we cannot do it in this instance because it is not known yet how it could be administered. The first person to respond was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. Quite rightly he realizes the implications of what we are about-would affect the Income Tax Act. That is what we are dealing with in this particular bill.
The minister told the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands on Thursday night that the administration of this program does not affect the principle of how the Income Tax Act presently operates with regard to family income. Of course the argument we are getting this afternoon from the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the parliamentary secretary is that we cannot do the very thing the hon. member for Broadview suggests because we are not ready to make those kinds of changes to the Income Tax Act. It is quite interesting that the minister wants to have it both ways in this instance.
The hon. member for Broadview is proposing, supported by members on this side, the notion that if you make this change at least it should deal with people equally, whether they are married on a legal basis or have entered into some common-law relationship. On the other hand the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the parliamentary secretary say this cannot be done because it would have a serious impact on the Income Tax Act which they are not quite ready to amend.
December 4, 1978

I find the minister's logic highly inconsistent. She is trying to explain away a bad provision, one that is becoming more and more unacceptable to groups. I want the minister to know, if she has not already learned from her office, that the National Action Committee, a large umbrella organization representing some 140 various women's organizations across the country, wired the minister's office and others who are concerned with this. I want to put this on record so that the minister is not under any further illusions with regard to where the National Action Committee stands on this bill. I quote from their telegram of December 3:
Hansard November 30 cites NAC support for Bill C-10, but we have serious reservations as expressed in our letter of October 16.
We support the principle of redistribution through refundable tax credits but do not support it in family allowance because of the consequences for low income families. An annual lump sum refund is of doubtful help.

The minister has introduced a concept of family income that would operate under the Income Tax Act which has not been clearly thought through. As the parliamentary secretary stated very clearly today, it does not relate to the other provisions of the Income Tax Act. He put that on the record.
The parliamentary secretary supported the opinion stated last Thursday by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. He made the case more effectively than anybody could make it, that the problem of making this kind of change, and setting into law a principle which can now be extended indefinitely across a host of income tax policies, would have very serious repercussions for women.
If anything needed to be stated more clearly, I do not know what it would be than the language of a bill which simply assumes that forever and a day the dependent spouse in this situation would be a woman. Her income is going to be lumped in with that of the man for purposes of deciding what amount of tax credit will be available.
What we have here and what the minister is now recommending is that even though this is a provision which has not been very clearly thought through, we are going to make it worse. We are going to discriminate for those who have entered into a common-law relationship and against those who are married under the normal legal requirements. The minister has put herself and the parliamentary secretary in a very difficult situation in arguing today entirely opposite to what they argued last Thursday evening when defending the very principle at stake in this clause.

The Monarchy THE MONARCHY POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should not proceed with proposed changes in respect of the status of Her Majesty the Queen as Queen of Canada or in respect of the status of the position of Governor General of Canada as set out in Bill C-60 of the third session, or otherwise.
He said: I realize that many hon. members will feel that this motion is entirely unnecessary and maybe unwanted. However, in meeting and speaking with a number of persons across Canada this summer, I was made aware of the fact that Canadians for the most part want the Queen retained as Queen of Canada.
There has been considerable alarm in this country as a result of Bill C-60 over whether or not the government really intends to keep the Queen and her successors as monarchs of Canada. The government has replied, by stating in so many words, that it has no intention of getting rid of the Queen of Canada. However under this famous bill, Bill C-60 of the last session, most of the powers of the Queen were given to the Governor General. The Governor General was in fact to become an all powerful head of state. Surely this can mean nothing else but that the true intention was to phase out the Queen as Queen of Canada. The fact that there is an election in the offing should be no reason for an instantaneous but not necessarily lasting, change of intent.
It is my belief that, if we are to prove to all Canadians that they have responsible representation in Ottawa, we must not be afraid to allow this motion to come to a vote and to show publicly our individual feelings on the monarchy. Canadians have a right to know.
If this motion is talked out or defeated, like so many private members' motions, it will be clear evidence to all Canadians that members of parliament strongly oppose the Queen of Canada.
Let me point out to you the major reasons why Canadians feel the Queen of Canada should be retained as an integral part of our federal democratic system. First, the Queen as an hereditary figure provides Canada with a continuous, constant, stable head of state. No matter what kind of confusion takes place at the political level, in a constitutional monarchy, which we now have, we are assured of the continuous presence of a most able ruler. In an electoral system there is always a chance that the system will be stalemated. The presence of a constitutional monarch rules out the threat of a possible lack of government. Citizens in a democracy must be able to criticize and remove their leaders without fear that there will be no one to take over.
Second, the presence of a constitutional monarch takes away the struggle for power which occurs in so many countries and often leads to dictatorship. The Queen ensures freedom in Canada. After all, the system of a constitutional monarchy is certainly better than absolute leadership.
Third, elevation of rulers and the formation of courts and cliques is inevitable in governments of all kinds. A constitu-

December 4, 1978
The Monarchy
tional monarchy is not only less dangerous and less costly than most of them, it also limits, although it does not prevent, this tendency to form potentates and courts which neither democratic theory nor electoral practice have been able to diminish. The presence of the Queen of Canada ensures that first ministers are in second place and are not the sole authority.
Fourth, the Queen presents to Canadians an aura of humanity amidst the vast realms of governmental bureaucracy. She is above partisan politics in government. When a Canadian sees Her Majesty in our country, he or she does not have to wonder if she is visiting that certain portion of the country to get votes. The Canadian cannot lend political overtones to her phrases. The Queen is truly a head of state to be respected.
Fifth, since we in Canada are at present blessed with a constitutional monarchy, we are safeguarded by the fact that the Queen is head of the armed forces. Since the relationship with the Queen also gives us the privilege of belonging to the Commonwealth, we are assisted in many aspects of world affairs.
Sixth, the Queen is a symbol of unity in most parts of our country. Some Canadians from certain portions of the country are upset at the fact that the Queen is indeed a symbol. These persons are not impressed by the fact that we should have a head of state whom we share with other countries. However, there are many persons in our country who owe allegiance in some form to various outside heads of state. I am thinking here specifically of those who owe allegiance to churches with heads outside this country, or to businesses. May I also say that whether it is a Queen or not, heads of government, or the elected leaders, they will take to themselves, if they can, the prestige and power that is involved in a symbol. Elected leaders can just as easily assume the role of monarchs, but often in a less democratic manner. Part of the reason for Confederation and the union of this country was the common allegiance to the Queen and the common ties to the mother country. It is amazing, at this time of disunity in Canada, that certain persons would wish to be rid of a force which first united this country.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, there are indeed many reasons for retaining the present status of Her Majesty, the Queen of Canada. The Crown is like an iceberg-it displays only the tip of its size and importance to those in Canada. However, the Crown is a necessary factor in the preservation of our freedom. 1 maintain that the status of the Governor General should also be maintained as representative of the Queen, not acting as her right hand, though.
This is indeed a necessary and important motion in order that the present questioning attitude about the retention of the Queen of Canada-an uprising caused by the wording of Bill C-60-be answered. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is indeed a quandary over the fate of our monarchy in Canada, whether or not members of parliament prefer to recognize it. We as members of parliament owe it to the people of Canada to settle this controversy once and for all.
[Mr. Jones.)
Again I repeat that if this motion is defeated or talked out, it will be clear evidence to the people of this country that members of parliament strongly oppose the Queen of Canada. I hope sincerely that that is not the case.

Mr. Speaker, first and foremost I would like to thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to speak to this motion. 1 would like to say initially that I hope some of the things I will say will dispel any concern he has about the intentions of this government, or of members on this side of the House, or of parliament, for that matter. 1 would also like to dispel the thought he might have that this motion would have to come to a vote to prove anything like the oath of loyalty to the Queen which I myself have taken when 1 was one of her officers. I do not think any vote in the House would supersede that in any way, and I see no necessity for the motion to come to a vote.
Without getting into any detail or contradicting the hon. member, I would like to remind him that when he mentioned the Governor General being commander in chief as something new, it was in the early 1900s that the monarch, by letters patent, indicated to him that he was commander in chief. So we would not be doing anything new there.
The motion before us states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should not proceed with the proposed changes in respect of the status of Her Majesty the Queen of Canada or in respect of the status of the position of the Governor General of Canada as set out in Bill C-60 of the third session, or otherwise.
I presume that the hon. member, in using the word "status", refers to the Oxford dictionary definition of that term, namely, social position or rank or a person's relation to others as fixed by law. His motion appears to be redundant since the bill neither interferes with the status of the Queen nor with that of the Governor General, but rather confirms the continuation of the monarchy, with the Queen occupying Canada's highest office as head of state, and it makes clear the stature, importance, and singularity of the office of Governor General.
When Bill C-60 was presented to the House we were told that it would die on the order paper. This technique was used to permit wide-ranging discussions, we were told, so that when the bill is presented again all Canadians will have the opportunity to make comment and effect changes in the bill. I can guarantee to the hon. member, as has the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), that the government has not proposed, nor does it intend, any change or diminution of the role of the monarchy in our system of government. In the proposed constitutional amendment bill, we have attempted to set out for all Canadians to see and know, the present roles of the sovereign and her representative.
As "A Time for Action" indicated, we believe that a new constitution of Canada should be a mordern document which would define the form of government and political structures chosen freely by all Canadians. Wherever possible, the written constituiion should reflect current rather than past constitu-
December 4, 1978

tional practice. Therefore, in the constitutional amendment bill the government has attempted to write into the constitution the present theory and practices regarding the monarchy. Because of the complexity and subtlety of this subject, this has not been an easy thing to do, and it was not possible or practical to attempt to cover all aspects of the subject. However, the constitutional amendment bill would confirm the continuation of the monarchy with the Queen occupying Canada's highest office as head of state, and would codify the reality of the Governor General's present powers as they have actually evolved, and make clear the stature, importance and singularity of his office.
All the essentials of our system of constitutional monarchy would remain. Indeed they would be clarified, and as a result, strengthened. As sovereign and head of state, the Queen would continue to appoint the Governor General. Also as constitutional monarch she could assume when visiting Canada any of the functions of the Governor General under the bill. The Government of Canada would continue to be carried on in the Queen's name.
The sovereign's representative, the Governor General, virtually would exercise all royal powers except the appointment of the holder of his office. He would exercise them on the basis of statutory constitutional provisions which have been derived from a variety of present sources of constitutional authority.
By consolidating and clarifying both the office of Governor General and the position of the sovereign, in accordance with existing practices, the bill would confirm the respective roles of the sovereign and the Governor General. Existing conventions protecting the Crown from political interference would not be weakened. On the contrary, the bill would secure in our constitution all the protection which now exists by convention for the maintenance and functioning of Canada's system of constitutional monarchy and responsible parliamentary democracy.
Surely the hon. member is aware that the Speech from the Throne delivered on October 11, 1978, indicated the following:
The government's view was and remains that the new constitution should describe the situation as it exists today in Canada, and the government is pleased that the provincial premiers expressed the same view during their meeting in Regina. There is no intention to change or to reduce in any way the role Her Majesty plays.

Therefore, at this very moment he is dealing with the provinces in discussing how the wording can achieve the intention of the government.

We have indicated many times that our intention was not to change the role of the monarchy. We indicated that as far back as 1968 when we published the white paper on the constitution. We have repeated it constantly since then that that was our intention.

I cannot understand the thinking of anyone who would entertain the idea of removing the Queen as head of our state, or in any way downgrading her position as leader of our people. As a matter of fact Bill C-60 did that, as has been recognized by certain authorities. The hon. member cast aspersions on the hon. Senator Forsey and the right hon. Roland Michener, a former Speaker of this House, who gave testimony before the Senate committee to the effect that Bill C-60 had an effect of downgrading the role of the monarchy and increasing the purpose of the Governor General at the Queen's expense, i do not think Senator Forsey and Mr. Michener should be classified as self-styled experts. I think they are recognized experts in the field of constitutional law. Certainly the former governor general has a good background for stating what the practical effects of Bill C-60 would have been.
The reaction of people across the country is not merely a sentimental reaction to an honoured and long standing tradition. Nor is it simply a love of symbolism or a standing in awe of all the pomp and ceremony which accompany any crowned head. There is a fear and a suspicion on the part of the people

that the government is doing something it should not be doing in this area. Some people in this country are actually afraid that if the Queen is shoved aside the way will be open for dictatorship or, at the least, republicanism of the kind we have seen fail time and time again in other countries. Since this government has already reflected dictatorial tendencies on occasion, that fear is very real in the minds of Canadians who have been observing this government for the past ten years.
Hundreds of thousands of people in Canada are rightfully suspicious of this government for ever suggesting any degree of tampering with the monarch's Canadian connection, and there has been an effort to tamper with it. I cannot believe that the drafters of Bill C-60 could be so inept and incompetent as to attempt to do what they did if that was the basis of what they were doing. I think there was more than ineptness and incompetence in the drafting of that bill.
The monarchy today is much more than a symbol of authority. As my hon. friend across the way and the mover of this motion have stated, it represents unity among peoples, brotherhood among nations and, therefore, it is a form of leadership. The monarchy stands as a form of popular leadership and the Queen is the physical personification of that leadership. She shows the kind of leadership everyone in Canada can look up to, regardless of political ideology. In other words, she unifies us. If ever this country needed that kind of leadership, it is now, because at this time there is certainly no leadership being provided by the present government. Canadians today need and want strong, popular leadership untainted by political ambitions toward dictatorship, and immune to the chance results of election campaigns based on promises which may never be kept.
Canada needs the kind of leadership that serves as a strong unifying force, and as the years roll by and as elections come and go, it is becoming more and more apparent that we are not getting that kind of leadership from currently practising politicians.
The monarchy provides us with continuous popular leadership and the continuous presence of an able and understanding leader. The monarch is always there, no matter how often our zealous politicians talk themselves out of office. We cannot be totally without government as long as the Queen remains the Queen of Canada. Nor are we left at the mercy of poorly managed government as long as she is there. She is our final appeal for true leadership.
As my hon. colleague has mentioned, the Queen ensures freedom in Canada: freedom to think, speak and act as we please within the letter of the law; freedom to worship as we see fit; freedom to live our lives usefully and with some hope of reward and satisfaction; and freedom to move about as we wish in our own country and to seek out greater opportunities for ourselves and for our families. Without the long shadow of the monarchy standing over it, no Canadian government can be held for very long to the responsibility for and the protection of all these freedoms which our people now enjoy.
December 4, 1978

Without the monarchy, sooner or later some ambitious oaf will show up and grind us under his dictatorial heel. It has happened in other countries, and it can happen here.
Indeed, the presence of the Queen in Canada serves as a very real reminder that first ministers are in second place, as my colleague has pointed out, and not in sole authority. We all know that some first ministers need to be reminded of that fact.
There is today an uprising in Canada, a surge of both emotional and rational reaction to this government's efforts at unseating the Queen of Canada. If we do not listen to the people now and heed their wishes in this respect, the day when we will wish we had will not be far off.
We must maintain the Queen's Canadian connection because she represents the only true leadership and the only unifying force available to us at this time. I again urge hon. members not to let their enthusiasm for the monarchy use up the remainder of our time. Let there be a real indication of where members of this House stand on this issue, because it is an important issue. 1 think the people of Canada are entitled to know where we stand. We should not cop out by letting our time expire as a means of denying the people of Canada the right to know where their members of parliament stand on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to quote part of motion No. 4, as follows:
-should not proceed with proposed changes in respect of the status of Her Majesty the Queen as Queen of Canada or in respect of the status of the position of Governor General of Canada as set out in Bill C-60-
Mr. Speaker, after hearing the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones) speak to us on his motion, when a French-Canadi-an hon. member from Quebec rises, one must surely wonder what he will say about motion like that one, especially as a French-Canadian from Quebec.
I might be well advised to say first of all why an hon. member from Quebec should want to participate in the debate on such a motion. First he does so to point out to the hon. member for Moncton that we Quebeckers are first of all French-speaking Canadians and, like Her Majesty the Queen, we have the advantage of being perfectly bilingual. My colleague across the way, the mover of this motion, has not had it seems, I shall not say the courage but the advantage of learning the two languages; we all know why he sits as an independent.
But we also know full well that his motion is but an excuse to hold a debate, for he is aware that we have a bill and white papers on the subject, and that the subject of his motion is already the topic of discussions across Canada. So he comes to us with some form of threat, saying that if we talk out the bill by discussing it until six o'clock, or if the vote is not taken
The Monarchy
before six, it will mean that we are against not only the motion, not to speak of the Queen, but also against the office of Governor General. Mr. Speaker, that in the vernacular is known as blackmail, and I will have none of it. About that motion proposed by the hon. member for Moncton known for his limping courage and supported by another independent member who unfortunately is one of my good friends, I do not know if he only intended to provide moral support so as to make it possible to debate the motion. The hon. member for Moncton knows very well that we share his belief although we come from Quebec or from other parts of the country. I would tell him what my grandfather said: Stop standing in front of the Queen, Mr. hon. member for Moncton, so that she might see us too, other Canadians. Some people out-Herod-Herod. The hon. member for Moncton reminds me of those.
If the hon. member for Moncton had taken time to read the statements by the Prime Minister-although I do not question his good faith-I begin to wonder if the hon. member has actually read the statement the Prime Minister made on the occasion of his visit to the Queen, he would know that the Prime Minister had had personal discussions with her when she came to Canada in October 1977. He then told her that he contemplated a study-I am using his own words-on the whole constitutional matter in 1978-79. It was not an obligation but a comprehensive study. We must never forget the difference between the consideration of a plan and compelling someone to take a decision which is beyond his judgment, his belief or his competence.
He also pointed out the importance of a renewed federal system. He did not say that is was essential to abolish a system or change the status of the Queen or that of the Governor General, but he merely emphasized the importance of a renewed federal system to counterbalance the campaign. I agree with the comments of the Prime Minister to counterbalance the campaign of the Quebec government trying to convince the people of that province to vote in favour of separation from Canada. Mr. Trudeau said to the Queen that in his opinion within a few years it would be essential to consider the constitution as a whole. It seems to me reasonable to ask such a thing, that is to consider the constitution as a whole with the provinces, to review some parts of it and to redraft an entirely Canadian document. Would it be a sin today to be Canadian? One can be Canadian today while clinging to some traditions, for example, the House of Commons, the democratic system, the English parliamentary system, which is the greatest democratic system in the world.
One may remain attached to the system, one may remain attached to the Queen of Canada without for that be deemed anti this or that. I have never read anywhere in the statements that anyone wanted to deprive the Queen of any powers, on the contrary if the process keeps on everyone will see- The hon. member stated that inevitably in the course of that debate certain questions would be asked about the relationship be-

December 4, 1978
The Monarchy
tween the Crown and Canada and about the functions of the Governor General. But that is what is being done tonight with the motion moved by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones). Moreover, the Prime Minister added that he and his government would do their utmost to make very sure that any debate or discussion not be a source of division in Canada. He does not prompt the participants in that debate to ask themselves whether it would be advisable to modify in depth the present status of the Crown in Canada.
We could go on like this for long but ultimately we will have to come back to the white paper called "A Time for Action" which mentioned various propositions contained in this motion. The Prime Minister also said at the time that he would table a letter addressed to the Queen and which she answered. Later the Prime Minister received from the Queen's private secretary a letter dated June 20-precisely the one my hon. colleague and the author of the motion was talking about a moment ago-which indicated that Her Majesty approved of the proposed changes in the royal titles and that she was convinced that these propositions would not change the basic nature of the relations between the Crown and Canada. Moreover, the Queen reiterated these remarks to the Prime Minister during audiences she granted him in Moncton last August 5.
But it seems to me that if we compare Bill C-60, which has been presented, and the study made in collaboration with the joint committee of the Senate and the House, the white paper "A Time for Action", as well as all the discussions and debates that have been going on since then between the premiers, there is no cause for alarm, even if we do not vote on this motion before six o'clock. It seems to me that we can rely on the sense of responsibility of the Prime Minister and the premiers as well as on the committee that was established to study the constitution.
I think that regardless of their political allegiance, the premiers are men elected by the Canadian people in each province. They are responsible men and, I repeat, despite their political allegiance, they are as Canadian and as responsible as the hon. member for Moncton can be. We ought to have confidence in these people, in the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada, who are studying and discussing the constitutional system to arrive at some kind of approach which will be more modern and more responsive to the needs of 1978-1979 and future years. But I do not see any scandal or concern about the hon. member's motion if the vote should be made after six o'clock.
Mr. Speaker, I do not see at all what the hon. member for Moncton wants, and this is why he irritated me at the beginning of his speech when he threatened us immediately, saying that if we talked until six it would mean-I do not want to repeat his words because they make me a little too angry. 1 shall let him repeat his own words on other occasions. But this is not how the government acts, it does not talk out bills for the sake of it. However, with this kind of meaningless motion,

when you know what is presently happening, I will not be disturbed if we reach six o'clock without having voted, I will not feel guilty and concerned about the result of his remarks after six o'clock either on television or on radio or whatever.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read again a quote from the right hon. Prime Minister on the adaptation, the renewal or the changes which will have to be made. He said, and I quote:
It is time to respond to this wish for renewal of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Moncton does not want to say or does not seem to be willing to say what the Prime Minister said at that time, at least he will believe a little what the people of Canada seem to be willing to say or what they have been saying up to now. The Prime Minister said: It is time to respond to this wish for renewal of the Canadian people. It is therefore up to parliament, the federal government, the provincial governments, as I said earlier, and all those in authority in our society to proceed so that this renewal will come about promptly, without mishap and in complete accordance with our democratic traditions. This could not be any clearer. There is no threat implied.
It is not a matter of passing legislation with a majority of votes to prevent the opposition-I do not even know if a Progressive Conservative member will rise later on to speak about this issue. 1 can see that two or three are here. In any case, there is no threat involved; the only thing that is involved is the action that we want to take because we believe that the Canadian population is ready to accept changes to our constitution. I believe that the Canadian people are not only ready for this, but that they have already waited too long. I believe that the people in this country are ready now to receive the changes that a courageous government will soon bring about. We are about to do so, and I hope that this problem will be solved long before the next election so that someone like me, who will probably not be in politics at that time, will be able to say: We have finally done something that the Canadian people have wanted for a long time.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Moncton cannot shame me into thinking that if there is no vote at six o'clock, everyone will regret it, not to repeat the words that he used. Certain formulas and the white paper were mentioned. People have often said that Canada cannot tolerate another decade of uncertainty. As I said earlier, in my opinion the Canadian people-and I say this as a French-speaking Canadian from Quebec-all the Canadian people, whether they are Englishspeaking or from another cultural background, are ready to accept the changes that we want to make. I do not have the impression that these changes will offend anyone as we want to maintain the authority of the monarch. Indeed, the bill never said that there was any desire to remove her powers. I do not know where the experts found this idea of a so-called change in power. Names were mentioned earlier. But I am starting to have some doubts as to whether these people were really well

known experts or whether they misread or read too rapidly the paper or the bill.
The government is adding to the legislation, which serves as a working document in the public, parliament and intergovernment debates. The coming months will improve the tone of the debate and accelerate the reaching of a consensus. It is apparent the Prime Minister at that time was far from desiring to remove any status from the Queen or the Governor General.
If we go back further, if we refer to the white paper in which were put forward the four main proposals for a renewed federation, and you probably know them better than myself, we find a re-statement of Canadian identity. There is nothing we could be more proud of. We want a re-statement of Canadian identity. I want to be called a French Canadian, a bilingual one. Call me anything, but call me a "Canadian". 1 will take pride in that. At the same time I am a Canadian citizen from the province of Quebec, and I feel I am as much a Canadian as my western colleagues who do not speak both languages, who at least did not have an opportunity to learn them, but who do not have the privilege to speak them, or who do not even make the effort to learn them.
Anyway this does not bother me at all. It does not shock me because there is as act on bilingualism, which affords us rather good protection as far as the public service and other services connected with justice and Canadian government are concerned. Therefore, those who are not bilingual do not shock me. But at least let them not act as though with their unilingual English language gave them a monopoly, not on "Canadianity" but almost, a monopoly on illustrations and famous Canadians, for the sole reason they are from the west or the east or the maritimes and they speak but one language. A Canadian is a fellow like myself who stands up and says what he thinks in the language he wants to use.
If they do not think I am saying it the right way, I can say it in English as well. To be a Canadian is not to be an Englishspeaking Canadian; it is to be a guy like me who learned the language during the war, not with the aid of books because I did not have that chance, but I made an effort and learned my English during the war. Maybe my English is not the best, but of course those English Canadians who taught me are to blame for that. However, I learned, I tried and 1 am very proud of that. It is not always from the grammar that you learn a language; it comes from the heart.
Hear, hear!

When you want to speak and you have it in your heart to do so, you succeed. Do not worry, Mr. Speaker, I do not care if the English I speak is broken or not, but there is one thing that is not broken inside me and that is my pride in being a Canadian. And that I shall remain.
The Monarchy

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of being able to speak on this motion presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones). This is private members' hour and I wish to advise hon. members that I do speak as a private member for Fundy-Roy-al, although I have no problem in my identification of the party that I represent in this House because, like myself, they agree there should be no dilution of the role of the monarchy or the Queen as head of state of this country.
Hear, hear!

Nevertheless I did become somewhat concerned when I heard the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) protest in a rather loud and inordinate way about the proposals introduced in Bill C-60. My feeling is that he is protesting too much. For what reason? I am concerned when members opposite and the government of this country begin to dabble in what we refer to as constitutional tinkering.
I am concerned that if there is no intention on the part of the government to dilute the authority of the monarchy in this country, why is it necessary to include any reference to this in Bill C-60? Bill C-60 very definitely states that the powers of the Queen are not to be diminished or diluted-words to that effect-while she is in Canada. That is absolutely contrary to my understanding of the constitution and the role of the monarchy in this country.
I intend to move along with my remarks and I will not take up the entire time allotted to me.
Canada has recently entered a period of reappraisal. Canadians feel that the time has come to reconsider what we are and to determine what we want to become. From the Atlantic to the Pacific we have been discussing our history and our future. We made a country out of a continent. It has been a great adventure. We built with our own hands a country stretching from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island, from Point Pelee to the northernmost reaches of the Arctic Islands. It took scarcely longer than a span of a man's life to do it. Many Canadians still remember the era of new settlements, the clearing of the lands, the great beginnings, the time when there were only five million of us, when our major cities- there were a dozen or so-had populations of barely more than 20,000, and when the railway and a handful of newspapers were the only means of linking region with region.
In order to adapt to the new continent, discover its spirit and learn to survive in its environment, our ancestors had to borrow the ways and customs of many peoples. But no custom and tradition has had more influence on the peaceful and orderly development of our great nation than the Crown. The Crown and the concept of constitutional monarchy have never been easy matters to explain. And because there is a tendency among all people to dismiss what they cannot easily explain, the monarchy in Canada has frequently been tossed off as either an historical anachronism that should long ago have gone the way of knights and round tables, or a stale leftover of colonialism, the fact being that we are a sovereign, independent nation with a foreign-that is, British-head of state.

December 4, 1978
The Monarchy
I submit that such a description of the Queen of Canada is a highly simplistic explanation of her function which is used to advantage by those who wish to erode the functions and traditions of the parliamentary system of government in Canada. Elizabeth II is the personal expression of the Crown of Canada, not the Crown of England. She is the Queen of Canada as well as the Queen of England and is the constitutional monarch of Canada. It is this combination that explains her role as head of state and as an institution of the Canadian government.
We note immediately that the Queen plays the same role in many other parts of the Commonwealth, and we face the question of a shared Crown and head of state. What is the advantage in modern times of this arrangement? Does it limit or compromise the sovereignty of Canada as an independent nation? This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I wish to examine these questions with you.
The Commonwealth serves 850 million people and includes huge nations and tiny states. Of its 33 members, all recognize the Queen as head of the Commonwealth. Sixteen new states plus India are republics with their own heads of state distinct from the Queen; 11, including Canada, are monarchies with the Queen as head of state; and five, all new states, are monarchies with monarchs other than the Queen as head of state.
Much has been written and said about the Commonwealth and 1 feel one particular attribute is worthy of mention this evening. That particular attribute is the ability of the Commonwealth to allow its member nations to participate in the orderly transition from colony to nation, the one singular force allowing such peaceful transition being the Crown.
Over the centuries many nations have conquered many other nations and developed lands into colonies. But they have rarely been inclined either to give easily the fruits of their conquests in development, or to admit to accusations of exploitation. The gaining of nationhood by dependencies has usually required a long process of negotiation, perhaps rebellion, and the aftermath may be bitter. As far as Britain's original dependencies were concerned, there were struggles but in the separation of the control of the mother country there was a stage which permitted a gradual, peaceful and face-saving change to independence under the Crown.
The British learned their lesson when the American colonies broke away, and since then they have followed a natural process comparable to the experience of any child who grows beyond dependence upon his parents, becomes able to support himself and handle his own affairs, and maintains an independent family relationship. Other empires disintegrated leaving little friendship either among the parts or between them and the original mother country. Such was not the case with the British Empire.
Canada, being a member of that British Empire, was able to weaken and then sever all governmental connections with Britain until she had complete control of her own affairs. Colonial status changed to dominion status and then to

independent status when conditions in Canada justified the change.
The existence of the Crown permitted face-saving on both sides. The provinces got all the trappings, symbols and ceremonies early to make them appear more grown up, even when there was little else to justify their identities. The government of the mother country saved face every time it gave up some power because the old links appeared at first to remain. But the old links did not remain and when everyone on both sides of the Atlantic realized it the Crown became a symbol, not of colonialism but of nationhood.
The Queen and the Crown therefore represent, among other things, the origin and growth of government. It was the Crown that gave out the original letters patent which gave the colonies their official status and served as a mark of sovereignty when they desperately needed to provide legitimacy, and this remained as a constitutional umbrella under which they grew to maturity. This shared heritage of the Crown was very important for it was in the midst of this tradition, even before colonies were politically stable, that the Crown helped to bring three of them together as four provinces in 1867 when they had little else in common besides their allegiance to a common sovereign. On their own initiative and terms they set up another central system with the same structure they had known for so long.
Then the new structure developed further on a national scale and this system was continued or set up in six new provinces. Meanwhile the constitution remains stable in a century when constitutions elsewhere were created and destroyed in reckless fashion, until now Canada's government is one of the oldest in the world and, as we have noted, her people have enjoyed, by global standards, a remarkable freedom from real political trouble.
All this did not take place because Canadians were superior people. They have a system that transplanted well in their environment and then worked. The question which we must now ask is what attributes of constitutional monarchy have made it work so well once it was transplanted in Canada. 1 suggest that a prime minister in Canada or a provincial premier is made to know from the start of his administration that he is advising on the use of the Queen's power, not wielding power that he actually possesses. There is an enormous practical difference between these two concepts. However much the Prime Minister can do on advising on the use of power, and even though he is among the most powerful, responsible heads of government in the world, he is always in the democratic position of being merely a trustee; and he knows it because of frequent and colourful reminders. He is a trustee to whom much responsibility can be entrusted but also readily taken away. It clearly puts the Prime Minister and his cabinet on the defensive at election time in an era when several heads of government elsewhere possess so much power that they are able to control elections or abolish them altogether.
The Crown has therefore a means of meeting a difficulty- so evident in history and contemporary politics throughout the world-that of preventing officials at the summit of govern-
December 4, 1978

merit from becoming too powerful, irresponsible and perhaps immovable.
This brings us to a definition of what the Canadian constitutional monarchy is all about. After centuries of political evolution we have arrived at the stage where all the powers of the state are vested, not in the state-that is, the formal governing structure-but in the community, with the person chosen to symbolize or personify those powers having no or scant powers to wield at all. That is, we separate the possession of power from the wielding of power. One institution, the monarchy, possesses the power without wielding it; the other institution, government, wields the power without possessing it.
Even though we may associate executive power with certain officials under our present constitution, we do not in law or in fact make it the personal possession of any of them. We put it outside the government structure, not in someone's hands but in an abstraction, and we call that abstraction the Crown.
The Crown, therefore, is not the monarch. The Crown is the people, and the monarch symbolizes the people, with all the dignity, stature, mystique and aura of her office. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once told her at a state dinner, "I always like being seen in public with you; it's the only time 1 never get booed"!
Oh, oh!

Those are the Prime Minister's words, not mine. If hon. members get complaints, take it up with the Prime Minister. Some of those opposite who are interested in retaining the monarchy have an awful lot to say when someone on this side is interested.

"God save the Queen" really means "God help us to govern ourselves". "God save the Governor General" does not sound so convincing. I urge that this motion not be talked out but that the question be put forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to oppose this motion. There is not an ounce of truth in the sentiments expressed in it. The motion of the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones) says that the government should not proceed with proposed changes with respect to the status of Her Majesty the Queen of Canada or with respect to the status of the Governor General as set out in Bill C-60.
I am not aware of where the hon. member for Moncton was for the summer months. He obviously was not in Ottawa attending meetings of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee. If he had been, he would have found out, as reiterated in this House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)
The Monarchy
and others on this side, that this government has no intention whatsoever of changing the role of the Queen or Governor General. In Bill C-60 the government was trying to codify the role of the monarchy and Governor General as it now exists.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) raced through his words as if he was ashamed to have this House ponder them for a moment. He stated that Bill C-60 should not have mentioned the Queen and her role, that it should have been silent. As the Prime Minister told the House, if the government had omitted any reference to the Queen in Bill C-60 it would have been charged with being anti-monarchist.
The role of the monarchy has changed over the years. In 1947 there were letters patent which changed the role of the monarch with regard to the signing of treaties. There have been other changes over the years.
I might point out that the Queen acquiesced to the sentiments of the government in Bill C-60. She was fully in agreement; she was not alarmed like the Tories.
I find it ironic that it is the hon. member for Moncton who has had the intestinal fortitude, otherwise known as guts, to bring this motion before this House of Commons. We know where he stands on the monarchy. I respect his views.
It is the Tory members who should have introduced this motion. They should have been leading the argument. However, the Tories like to have it both ways. They have done this country irreparable harm in the way they have dragged the honourable name of Her Majesty the Queen and the institution of the monarchy through the mud of Canadian politics over the last six months. It is not the government that is mucking around with the monarchy; it is the Conservative party which is trying to make political hay out of this issue.
Hear, hear!

I should like to deal with the most recent arguments put forward by the Minister of Finance, his parliamentary secretary, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. For example, the payment of the credit can be manipulated so that it is given at a politically opportune time. It is no secret that a large sum of money ranging from $200 to $1,200 will be going to recipients right across the country in the spring of 1979. It is of no surprise that the government is reluctant to put into the law a system which would regularize the payment.
According to the evidence given by the National Indian Brotherhood and the national anti-poverty organization, the payment would tie the hands of the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance and tell them that they cannot manipulate the system in that manner. We on this side of the House are very aware of what we are receiving: a large bundle of goodies which will go out to the people of Canada in April. Perhaps they will not be distributed in the most beneficial manner from the points of view of those people, and perhaps they will not be doing the most good in the long run.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, there is no provision in the Income Tax Act for an overpayment to be made over time. There is a firmly established practice in the Income Tax Act that when the government owes an overpayment to an individual, that payment is owing in total when it is due. There is no provision in the Income Tax Act for the delay of an overpayment over time. The only way to ensure that this benefit will be paid in a regular quarterly sum and not be subject to administrative or

political abuse is that it be written in the law that this payment will be made on a quarterly basis, rather than making a lump sum payment.
If we are looking for a socially responsible tax credit scheme which will allow low income families to budget for an increase in their payments over time, then I suggest very strongly we must move to a quarterly system rather than a lump sum system. Why must we wait for a year or two for the minister to see the political or social repercussions of this matter? Why can we not move to the other system? The answer is very simple: it is because the election is coming up.
My second point relating to the lump sum payment deals with tax discounters. As far as my party is concerned, we see the lump sum payment as a windfall benefit to income tax discounters. It was never anticipated, at the time the income tax discount bill was passed last year, that there would be 1.5 million new low income filers waiting for a large cheque from the government in April. The income tax discount bill was passed at a time when the only moneys to be received were overpayments on one year's wages which would be rebated to individuals. It was never anticipated that the overpayments to be paid out would be in the range of $200, $400, $600, $800 or $1,000. Therefore, the passage of the lump sum payment guarantees a subsidy of a very sizeable nature. We are talking about millions of dollars of benefit to the income tax discounters of Canada. That windfall benefit was never anticipated at the time the income tax discount bill was passed. All of us who represent people in low income districts know this is the case.
As friendly and open as the government has been to our suggestions, the lack of response to this very real problem is a disgrace. Quite honestly, I say to the minister that none of the explanations provided have been satisfactory.
We are looking for a system that provides legal guarantees to people that there will be regular quarterly payments on which they can budget and in respect of which they can see their incomes growing over time. We are talking about people living on welfare, or close to living on welfare, making a minimum wage, and suddenly receiving $1,000 or $1,200 from the government. The government is putting this forward as a socially responsible tax scheme. It is not that; it is an irresponsible scheme because it guarantees that much of this money will be wasted, that much of it will get into the hands of people on the outskirts or the fringes of the financial community in this country who do not deserve it and should not be getting the money. This money should be going to the people who are in need on a regular quarterly basis. This is what is wrong with the scheme, Mr. Chairman.

Family Allowances
people in my constituency depend on their family allowance cheques to a large degree in order to purchase groceries or clothing for their children. Particularly larger families with five or six children depend on that approximately $25 every month in order to meet expenses, such as light bills or heat bills in the winter time. Some cabinet members and members of the Conservative party have indicated that money does not grow on trees, and that the deficit is already large enough. I believe ordinary Canadians, particularly low income earners, deserve a larger piece of the pie or more money.
As was pointed out by John Gray in an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on Saturday, in the last ten years the bottom 20 per cent of the population received less than the national income. Now they receive less of the national income than they received ten years ago.
I know this bill is a progressive one. It is doing the right thing. It will put more money in the hands of low income Canadians via the tax credit. But I cannot see why the basic amount of family allowance has to be reduced at the same time. Canada can afford the tax credit and the current rate of family allowance quite easily. All members are concerned about stimulating the economy and creating more jobs. If money is put in the hands of ordinary people, they will spend it purchasing consumer goods such as food, clothing and the like. Most of these goods are labour intensive in nature. It would provide jobs and assist in stimulating the economy. It would prime the pump at the bottom. It would not be the old trickle down theory where a few big carrots are offered to a company in the hope that a few more jobs will be created. It would provide ordinary people with money. I am referring to the people on the street, in the neighbourhoods, and on the farms.
