Mr. Speaker, the question I should like to deal with tonight arises from questions I posed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on November 10 as they appear at page 1007 of Hansard for that date. They related to the movement of grain to export positions. They arose also from the statement of officials of the Canadian Wheat Board that some 2.3 million tonnes in grain sales had been deferred this year, meaning ultimately a loss of income to the farmers of something of the order of $350 million. It was also stated that some four million tonnes of additional export sales could have been realized in the last crop year if sufficient transportation capacity had been made available, and this amounted to a loss of $500 million.
The Minister of Agriculture in his response to me at that time suggested I was engaged in sweeping accusations, that the situation was being watched closely, and he implied that it was easy to make sweeping accusations but difficult to deal with the problem.
At that time I went on and tried to elicit from him whether the government had any action or plan to increase grain-handling capabilities in order to meet the challenges of the 1980s and, specifically, the challenges which will presented on the west coast, resulting in demand for an increased capacity of something of the order of 70 per cent. There was the usual waffling answer from the Minister of Agriculture indicating that new programs were being worked on, etc.
These questions and this kind of answer are not new in this House. What is becoming increasingly disturbing is the fact that conditions are deteriorating day by day. What we on this side find difficult to comprehend is why the minister and the government are so touchy and so much on the defensive when we raise these issues. They attempt to disregard the magnitude and importance of the matter of grain handling and the transportation system, and engage primarily in rhetoric rather than dealing specifically with answers to the questions.
Adjournment Debate
Again today in the House I brought up a situation which clearly demonstrates a failure on the part of someone-and I am not going to point any finger here-engaged in the grain handling and transportation business regarding a total lack of co-ordination in respect of the allocation of railway rolling stock. There has been a complete breakdown. We now have the situation of empty cars being despatched to country elevator points for which there are no orders. Because there are no orders these railway cars eventually end up in the hands of the railways, empty. There is a complete breakdown in utilization. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was disturbed and irate, and attempted to twist and distort the question I posed to him this afternoon. He attempted furthermore to try to subvert a reasonable solution which we on this side of the House had proposed.
The fact is that Canada continues to lose sales every day; and the fact that the situation deteriorates day by day is why this matter should be raised in the House every day and why we should be demanding action. Last week the Canadian Wheat Board had to withdraw from the monthly market of the Japanese food agency. The fact is that the United States has now captured a good percentage of our traditional Chinese market and is vigorously pursuing other markets.
It is an additional fact that the Alberta Wheat Pool and other grain companies are now engaged in the movement of grain, particularly oilseeds, to the west coast because there is inadequacy of grain transportation, specifically railway cars. This is a very expensive proposition. The fact that these things are taking place would indicate there is a very serious problem. It is a fact that the barley producers are suffering because markets have literally come to an end, not because there are no possibilities of sales but because there is an inadequate transportation system in place to move that grain. As of this date some 2.3 million tonnes of grain sales have been deferred, and more sales are being deferred every day. I am sure that the total must now amount to at least half a billion dollars.
We have demurrage charges. Our reputation as a reliable supplier of grain continues to deteriorate. We are told that the rapeseed industry is threatened by the fact that there is a billion dollars' worth of export sales which cannot be delivered at this time. These are some of the reasons we are demanding action from this government.
I submit that the reason the ministers responsible find our questions offensive is failure on the part of their government to deliver the goods which they promised, specifically the promises of the 1974 election. There is a failure on the part of the government to act even at this late date on what I refer to as an emergency situation. The Minister of Transport talks of more studies. He talks of the necessity for technical analysis. The system has been studied to death. Surely we do not require technical analysts to come here from the United States to try to figure out what is wrong, when railway cars are being despatched to country elevator points where there are no orders. Surely we do not require that kind of expertise.

Adjournment Debate
As far as we are concerned, there is only one way to resolve this matter today, and that is to bring together representatives of the components which are involved in the grain handling, transportation and marketing systems. Surely the combined expertise of these individuals, with proper leadership and a desire on the part of government, can serve as a catalyst for current planning and for the future. We must stop this political rhetoric and get on with some action, because if the problems are not resolved soon, the tragedy of the 1970s will be the loss of Canada's prominence in the world export grain trade picture.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question was thoroughly debated in the House on November 13, but I will repeat the minister's position for the hon. member's benefit.
This government has been concerned for a great number of years about the problems facing the grain transportation and handling system, and we have numerous programs in place to alleviate these problems in the years ahead. These programs are aimed at achieving precisely the same target as that outlined recently by the commissioners of the Canadian Wheat Board. The minister has for several years spoken about "building for a billion" in our programs in support of the grain transportation system. He has more recently spoken about exports in excess of a billion bushels as achieved by the mid-1980s.
But this minister has also done much more than merely talk about the problem. He has instituted solid programs to rescue the transportation system from the rapid deterioration it was subject to following half a century of neglect. Some hard decisions have had to be made, and he has had the courage to make them.
The network of rail lines has been trimmed down to a supportable size, and we are in the process of rehabilitating these lines. Some $100 million has already been spent on this program, and it will have cost in excess of $700 million when it is completed in the mid-1980s. These improvements cannot be made overnight, but we have moved to implement them as quickly as possible.
The fleet of rolling stock for the movement of grain has been gradually aging and taken out of service. This minister recognized this early and started purchasing new, modern hopper cars in 1973. The government has now purchased 8,000 hopper cars at a cost of $256 million.
Canada's grain terminal capacity is also being increased. Under the Canadian Wheat Board's storage incentive scheme, storage capacity at Vancouver is to be increased by 40 per cent. Half of this increased storage, 5.8 million tonnes, is to be completed in time to provide increased capacity in Vancouver this winter. The remainder will come on stream by the end of next year.
There are significant improvements that are being made today to increase our export potential now and in the future. We are also investigating every possible means available to move the maximum amount of grain through the St. Lawrence

system prior to the closing of that system, including increasing the hours of operation wherever possible.
But we are not concerned just about the immediate problems we are facing. We are also concerned about the long-term problems facing the grain handling and transportation systems. We have had the Hall commission inquire into the complex social and economic relationships involved in this system. We are now very near to having in place a complete basic network of prairie branch lines that are guaranteed operation until the year 2000. This provides the grain companies with the necessary certainty of service so that they can confidently proceed with the replacement and upgrading of facilities so necessary to provide farmers with the facilities they require.
The federal government is also proceeding with a program of rehabilitating those branch lines that are designated as part of the basic network. This program has seen the commitment of $170 million for the first three years and will see the expenditure of $700 million before it is completed. Improvements to various rail lines in the pairies are already available for all to see.
Once this program is completed, all the basic network lines will be capable of carrying hopper cars that will travel at speeds far in excess of those permitted today. These improvements will provide the capacity necessary to carry the increased volumes of grain necessary in the future.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we are moving to provide the necessary capacity. We are building a system capable of moving in excess of a billion bushels by the middle of the 1980s. It is not a process that can be expected to occur overnight but all the necessary programs are in place now.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT-DELAY IN SOLVING TAXPAYERS' PROBLEMS
NATIONAL REVENUE-REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT-DELAY IN SOLVING TAXPAYERS' PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 28 I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) whether it was a correct interpretation of an article that appeared in the Globe and Mail on November 22 that, as a result of the decentralization of operations of the Department of National Revenue, the service to the public in a number of cases would be less efficient and not more efficient.
The report in the business section of the newspaper stated that the director general of the compliance division of the Department of National Revenue, Mr. J. L. Gourlay, had said in a speech to a group of tax accountants in Montreal that the result of decentralization would be to provide a better service for a larger number of accounts than could be handled in the local office; and where there was a problem, reference would have to be made to the centralized records kept at head office in Ottawa and there would be delay in providing the service.
The minister's reply to my question in the House, as reported at page 1565 of Hansard, seemed to admit that in perhaps
December 4, 1978

75 per cent to 80 per cent of cases there would be good service but in the remaining cases there might be further delays.
This raises the whole question of the objectives of the government in the decentralization program that is being implemented and the results of the program. I cannot help but refer to a speech made during the budget debate by my colleague on this side of the House, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) in which he dwelt at considerable length on the need to go ahead with decentralization. He pointed out that when the policy was announced by the then president of the treasury board, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), in May 1975, the objectives were, first, to bring the administration of federal programs closer to those directly concerned; second, to help slow growth and high unemployment areas; third, to make the federal administration more conspicuous in communities where it was not much felt and where activities related to the country as a whole can contribute to national unity; and, finally, to reduce the undue concentration of civil servants in the national capital area. In the national capital region there are fewer than 25 per cent of the entire public service of this country. How this figure can be construed as an "undue concentration" in the national capital is something 1 fail to understand.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke went on to say that the total capital expenditures required by government for the decentralization program will amount to some $200 million. He said that this will not require additional expenditures since most are charged against the normal construction budget of the Department of Public Works. I offer that as an interesting example of double talk. Without question the program is more expensive. New buildings have to be built and they are costly. The hon. member for Sherbrooke referred to man-years and said this was a great thing. He pointed out that 24 Canadian cities had been selected to receive the transfer of federal employees. As reported at page 1447 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
For the sake of political decency, we cannot let the hopes of a whole population hang in midair without knowing what will happen.
1 agree, Mr. Speaker. He went on to say as follows:
The federal government is determined to relocate that service in Sherbrooke, in accordance with the commitment given to the public servants and all the provinces in the house in 1974. Let us think about it: it concerns 750 employees, plus their spouses and children, a total of about 2,000 people. It means creation of at least 1,500 direct and indirect jobs, total annual wage of over $15 million, and capital investments in the range of $40 million. In brief, a project with absolutely tremendous economic repercussions.
I cannot help but observe that in days past when an army attacked a city, they circled it, pillaged it and took the booty home. Nowadays some members of a political party think they can pillage and take booty away from the national capital and treat it in about the same way invading armies did centuries ago.
My colleague from Sherbrooke referred to the costs. We now have restraint in government expenditures. Surely these costs to which he refers cannot be justified. I say to my
Adjournment Debate
colleague from Sherbrooke that the decentralization program was conceived at a time when there was an average federal growth of 3 per cent in the public service. Now we do not have zero growth but negative growth. In the national capital region are 65 per cent of those 5,000 positions that are to be declared redundant, and we have one-quarter of the federal public service in the national capital region.
I stress to my colleagues and friends on all sides of the House the impact of decentralization and relocation on the city of Ottawa. In the central business core of the city, 6 million square feet of office space will be vacated by the federal government as a result of this shift in its operations. Two million square feet of temporary structures will be destroyed. Four million square feet of privately-owned accommodation will be vacated. Vacancy rates are approaching 15 per cent to 20 per cent in the central core, and will approach 30 per cent before very long. The national capital itself, as a result of the diminution of the federal grant and the removal of federal activities, will probably suffer the highest real estate taxes of any metropolitan community in Canada.
I simply point out that the policy of decentralization was conceived in other circumstances and cannot be applied in the way the announcement indicated it would in 1975. The policy is costly, it is wasteful and it is inefficient. It has an undue impact on one region, the capital city. I ask that this policy be reconsidered.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT-DELAY IN SOLVING TAXPAYERS' PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reorganization, or more properly the decentralization, of the operations of the Department of National Revenue, Taxation, was initiated as part of the government's decentralization program. Hon. members will be aware of a number of other instances in which the government has moved or is in the course of moving operations from Ottawa to other locations in Canada to create greater opportunities for employment and to increase the federal presence.
In the particular case of taxation, some decentralization is necessary for operational reasons. Every year during the period in which the mass filing and initial processing of tax returns takes place, the department has had to hire several thousand temporary employees who could be expected to achieve a high degree of efficiency in data conversion and associated clerical work at its single processing centre in Ottawa. With the growth in the volume of tax returns it was becoming very difficult to find enough temporary workers of the kind needed in Ottawa. As an interim measure a second and temporary centre was set up in Winnipeg.
Longer term plans to spread the work more evenly were approved which called for the construction of six permanent centres. They are to be called taxation centres. One is to be located in Surrey, B.C., one in Shawinigan-Sud, Quebec- both of which have recently been opened-and four more to be located in Winnipeg, Manitoba, St. John's, Newfoundland, Jonquiere, Quebec, and Sudbury, Ontario. As a last stage the Ottawa processing centre would be converted to the new mode, making seven taxation centres in all.

December 4, 1978
Adjournment Debate
At the same time, it was seen that to have almost entirely temporary work at these centres would not be a satisfactory answer to employment creation as would a good mixture of temporary and permanent work. Therefore it was decided to move not only the initial processing from Ottawa to the centres but also certain work from the 28 district offices which did not require direct contact with the public. In so doing we would provide more permanent jobs at the taxation centres and have opportunities for efficiency through economies of scale.
The taxpayer should experience no decrease in the level of service. Most taxpayers' contact with the department of taxation is by mail. In general the centres, when spread geographically, should be more responsive than was possible with one centre in Ottawa. The district offices will remain where they are to answer the inquiries of those who seek information by phone or by personal visit.
It is true that the individual taxpayer's files now in the district offices will be held in the centres. However, less than 10 per cent of inquiries require reference to an individual file and measures will be taken for quick transportation of the files from the centres to the district offices when they are needed.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-ASYLUM IN CANADA FOR SOUTHEAST ASIAN REFUGEES
IMMIGRATION-ASYLUM IN CANADA FOR SOUTHEAST ASIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 I asked a question of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) concerning Vietnamese refugees. I asked the minister whether contacts had been made with the United Nations commissioner for refugee matters and what the status was regarding the acceptance by Canada of some of these refugees on the Hai Hong.
I think all Canadians have been concerned about what has been happening in that part of the world to those who have been forced to flee from their country. 1 suggest it is a desperate situation, and not only in Southeast Asia. I do not have time to do this tonight, but one could identify at least five or six areas in the world today where there is conflict and where refugees could be called forward or would want to come to Canada.
While we might say we have peace in the world, we have to keep in mind the fact that there are trouble spots. We have to respond as members of the international community. In fact, the United Nations commissioner for refugees estimates that the world's refugee problem could be in the order of ten million. Whatever the exact figures, the fact remains that at this point in the world's history we have the highest number of refugees and humanitarian cases since the last days of World War II. We all know the tremendous displacement of humanity which was the result of that human conflict, yet somehow today we have not felt the impact of similar numbers who can no longer live in their country.
Statistics and people who have studied this question show that the problem is not likely to decrease, numerically at least,

in the foreseeable future. In Thailand today there are 130,000 to 150,000 persons who are either refugees or are what are sometimes termed displaced persons. The small country of Malaysia has between 30,000 and 40,000 refugees. That is the situation. Daily people are leaving in unseaworthy craft or small fishing vessels. They are embarking on a search for freedom in a country which at that point in time they simply do not know but which might accept them.
Who is a refugee? We must first keep in mind that he or she is a person, a human being who has lost his home and ability to make a living. Very often it is a human being who has lost his or her family, or at least some members of that family.
In 1976 we passed the Immigration Act which was proclaimed this year. For the first time we placed into an Immigration Act in Canada the provision that we would accept refugees. This is part of Canada's immigration policy at the present time. We said we would accept as refugees those who were defined as conventional refugees. We would also accept humanitarian cases, people who might not be classed as conventional refugees but who are displaced by emergency situations of war, social upheaval or natural disaster.
There are those who say that refugees take jobs. They say they are not people such as we are. I want to say that these are people who are doers. They are builders. I had a teacher who often said to me that in life it is a risk to meet people, but a risk well worth taking. No better can we use that argument than with these refugees.
The natural flow for the next year has been defined by the minister as in the order of 100,000, of which 6,000 are to be refugees. Who is taking these refugees? The United States, France, Belgium, Australia and Canada. How about Sweden? According to statistics, they are not taking refugees from Southeast Asia yet that much maligned country, the United States, is taking a minimum of 25,000. Where are those who protested during the war? Where are they today? Is the suffering of humanity at the hands of a government, be it of the right or of the left, no longer important? Where, for instance, are the clips on television of people protesting the war that we saw in the sixties?
If all that was valid, how is it that the carnage in Southeast Asia today is not something we should protest? Where are the Berrigans today, where are the Fondas? Where are those who actively resisted the government? The genocide in Cambodia at the present time defies imagination. What about Vietnam? We do not hear reports of genocide in Vietnam as in Cambodia, but what about the people who are forced to leave Ho Chi Minh city and go into the countryside where they can find nothing to live on? What about the displacement of families? Is Vietnam setting up a gulag such as was described so well by the Russian writer Solzhenitsyn?
I am not protesting to the government, but surely in the name of humanity, as members of the international community we should look seriously at the responsibility we have as Canadians. We have taken 600 refugees from the Hai Hong.
December 4, 1978

That is commendable. 1 recognize we cannot solve the refugee problems of the world. What I am saying, hopefully with the support of a great many Canadians, is: let us be sensitive to the needs of these people and, having analysed the situation, recognize from a humanitarian point of view what our obligations should be in terms of settling people here, not only giving them the benefit of freedom but, as Canadians, ourselves getting the benefit of their drive and loyalty to this country.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-ASYLUM IN CANADA FOR SOUTHEAST ASIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be remiss of me if 1 did not, first of all, compliment the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) on his erudite commentary concerning the situation of these refugees in the world today. I agree wholeheartedly with his comments and I, too, look to Canada to show the way by adopting a humanitarian approach to this whole difficult question.
Canada and other concerned countries have for some time been in consultation with representatives of the U.N. high commission for refugees on the plight of the Hai Hong
Adjournment Debate
refugees. As a result of these discussions, the minister announced on November 18, 1978, that Canada was prepared to accept 600 of these people.
At the time of the announcement, the minister called upon church groups, service clubs, other groups and concerned Canadians in general for such as welcoming committees, accommodation, clothing, and other personal assistance in integrating these people into community life. The minister also indicated at that time that Canadian groups of five or more could sponsor Southeast Asian refugees. These would be in addition to the 600 announced, and the monthly commitment of 50 "small-boat escapee" and 20 Thailand "camp" refugee families.
I am confident that, as in the past, the Canadian people will demonstrate their charity in assisting and welcoming these refugees to their new home country.
